characters: Oppong: a nine-year-old Ghanaian boy with short neat hair in a yellow shirt and khaki-brown school shorts, holding a plain unlabelled notebook.
Naab: his ten-year-old Ghanaian classmate with neat braided puffs tied with yellow ribbons, wearing a yellow shirt and brown school pinafore, holding a wooden pencil.
Their teacher: a warm Ghanaian female Primary 4 teacher with braided hair in a bun, wearing a leafy green African-print dress.

narrationPlan.voice: A curious boy’s voice for Oppong; a quick-thinking girl’s voice for Naab
narrationPlan.pace: Steady, like a careful walk (about 100 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: A light walking tune with small animal sounds (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Hens, goats, agama lizards, and grasshoppers are seen in many Ghanaian school compounds. The story follows NaCCA Basic 4 Science standards on classifying animals and their life processes (B4.1.1.1.1, B4.1.1.1.2).
The frog is not forced into one of the four groups. It is named accurately as an amphibian to be studied later.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Check the features given for each group against NaCCA B4.1.1.1.1.
Check that the story treats the frog honestly as an amphibian outside the four groups.

teacherGuide.overview: An animal walk shows how to sort animals into insects, birds, mammals, and reptiles by their observable body features. Children also learn that all animals move, feed, and reproduce. Based on NaCCA Basic 4 Science.
learningGoals: Sort animals into four groups using observable body features.
Give at least one defining feature of each group.
Explain that all animals move, feed, and reproduce.

subjectLinks.subject: English
subjectLinks.link: Making and reading a classification table

beforeReading: Ask: how can we tell a bird from a lizard just by looking closely?
whileReading: Pause at each page and let learners name the body feature that decides the animal group.
afterReading: Sort picture cards into four groups and give reasons.
Act out how different animals move and feed.
discussion: Why does the frog not fit our four groups?
Why is it important for animals to feed and reproduce?
reflection: Which animal group surprised you most today?

support: Use picture cards with a key feature prompt on each.
stretch: Investigate an animal that surprises people—such as a bat—and explain why it is a mammal rather than a bird.

culturalNotes: Hens, goats, agama lizards, and grasshoppers are seen in many Ghanaian school compounds. The story follows NaCCA Basic 4 Science standards on classifying animals and their life processes (B4.1.1.1.1, B4.1.1.1.2).
The frog is not forced into one of the four groups. It is named accurately as an amphibian to be studied later.
localiseThis: Observe the animals found safely around your school compound.
Look, do not touch: some animals bite or sting. Wash hands with soap after the walk.

factCheck.claim: Insects have six legs and three body parts, birds have feathers and beaks, mammals have hair or fur and nurse young with milk, reptiles have dry scaly skin, and frogs are smooth-skinned amphibians.
factCheck.explanation: Matches standard vertebrate and invertebrate morphological classification taught in upper primary science.
factCheck.reference: NaCCA Science Curriculum for Basic 4 (B4.1.1.1.1 & B4.1.1.1.2).
